work.title: Life of Alexander, priest of Side (15 March)

paragraphs.text: And many believed in him. When the governor heard this, he ordered him to be brought in. When Alexander arrived, the governor said to him: “Tell me, who are you, deceiving so many and turning them away from sacrifices to the gods, and teaching them another faith? Tell us, then, who you are to deceive the people like this.” Alexander said, “I am a Christian, and my rank is that of a priest. In this office, governor, I have hoped through faith to receive what is hoped for in Christ.” Antoninus said, “And who is Christ?” Alexander said, “The Savior of the whole world, and the light of those who believe in him.” Antoninus said, “How can he be a savior when he was crucified and suffered death?” Alexander said, “This is the wonder, governor: that he died in the flesh, so that he might not only enlighten [?], but also free the dead from suffering in Hades.” Antoninus said, “You speak foolish words and much nonsense. How, then, can someone who could not help himself help others?” Alexander said, “His death gives those who believe in him life and imperishability in heaven.” Antoninus said, “Then stop speaking nonsense and sacrifice to the gods.” Alexander said, “I am not speaking nonsense when I say this. But if I obey you,

then I am not only deluded but a fool, for your words are foolish.” Antoninus said, “By the gods, if you obey and sacrifice to the gods, you will be the master of great wealth. But if you do not obey, I will destroy you with cruel tortures.” Alexander said, “Do not deceive yourself, governor, that I will listen to your flattery and miss Christ’s coming. For he is the living God.” Antoninus said, “If you do not sacrifice, I will display you before everyone under torture.” Alexander said, “I will die in cruel torments at Christ’s hands if I obey you and sacrifice to unclean demons.” Antoninus said, “Strip him and beat him on the belly with raw sinews.” While he was being beaten and saying nothing, the governor said to him, “Obey me, Alexander, and sacrifice to the gods.” Alexander said, “Your tortures are nothing, you tormentor, and I will not sacrifice. I have already told you that I am a Christian and that there is a God in heaven who helps me.” Antoninus said, “Did I not tell you to abandon this nonsense and come forward and sacrifice, so that the emperor’s will may be done?” Alexander said, “I offer sacrifice to the eternal King.” who made heaven and earth, and the sea and everything

in them. Antoninus said, “Do they not seem to you to be gods, those to whom the sovereign emperor himself offers sacrifices?” Alexander said, “Great amazement seizes me, governor. May we someday see even you yourself repenting of the deception of idols and turning to the truth.” Antoninus said, “Are you mad, Alexander?” Alexander said, “I am not mad, but I fear God and his Son Jesus Christ, who has power over soul and body on the day of judgment.” Antoninus said, “Kindle a fire and heat the pan, so that he may be thrown into it and his sorcery may thereby be overcome.” When the fire had been kindled, they heated the pan until it was like fire. Antoninus said to him, “Alexander, offer sacrifice, so that you do not end up in the pan. Christ, whom you worship, will be of no help to you.” Alexander said, “You are not saying this of your own accord, but at the prompting of your father Satan, through whose dignity you have been filled with wisdom.” Antoninus said, “Let him be thrown into the pan, so that I may see what help the one who was crucified and died will give him.” Alexander joyfully leaped into the pan. He went in alone, but he could be seen in the pan

as one of three. When he had entered the pan, dew came from heaven, and the pan became as though it had never known fire. Alexander was praising God and saying, “God, who reigns forever and sits upon the cherubim, whom the angels and archangels praise, I, the sinner, Alexander, bless you, because you worked wonders for your servant Daniel, shut the lion’s mouth, crushed all the power of his adversaries, and crowned your servant. Now also hear me, God, and show this Antoninus, who is unworthy of your blessings, that his hopes are intertwined with demons, who, being imperfect themselves, make those who hope in them imperfect.” Antoninus said, “I told you, Alexander, that you have a demon, and trusting in it, you feel no shame.” Alexander said, “Do you not understand, foolish man, that a demon is never tormented with such torments, but requires sacrifices and the fumes of useless sacrifices, which plunge people into destruction?” Having learned from him, you have become a teacher yourself and entered into a fiery kinship. And you make those tortured with you your companions.” Antoninus said, “Set four wooden posts in the ground, stretch him out along the posts, and bind

him tightly, so that, stretched out by the posts, he will be broken and offer sacrifice, or else, exposed, die a miserable death.” Alexander said as he was being tortured, “Your devices are nothing.” And Alexander was brought forward and stretched out on the posts. The valiant martyr of Christ endured such torture, seeing all his limbs stretched out and all his bones being broken. Speaking with great wisdom, Alexander said, “You are the God of the Christians, who have come to the saints who pleased you. Come also to me, a sinner, and show that your name is great and [?] those who fear you.” When he had said this, his face changed and became like a flame. One of those serving before the governor approached him and said to him, “It is clear to everyone, Alexander, that you are prevailing through sorcery. For your face looked pale, but now it is bright as the sun.” Alexander said, “You rightly said it was pale, because of bodily weakness. For everyone suffering bodily pain grows very pale. But the brightness you now see is because of endurance and God’s providence. For everyone who endures is saved forever.” The servant said, “Then is it because of endurance that your face changes?” Alexander said, “Yes.

Learn this yourself, then, O man: every Christian who seeks hope in God will readily find it. For earthly wealth is obtained with toil and great suffering, and through it souls that lack self-restraint go to destruction. And many here are now seeking it. But wealth toward God comes quickly and brings thankfulness; it is easily obtained: the kingdom of heaven can be acquired not with gold or silver, but with lowly copper.” Hearing this, the servant said, “Guide me, I beg you, so that perhaps I too may be able to share in it forever and ever.” Alexander said, “Believe in God and in Christ, through whom you will have life forever and ever.” The servant said, “O God, who help your servant Alexander, help me also, a sinner. Draw me away from foul defilement, from the falsely named gods, and from their deception, and from the wrath of the ungodly Antoninus, the author of every evil. And count me among your servants together with your servant Alexander.” And Alexander said, “O God, may your will be done in answer to your servant’s prayer.” The governor heard his prayers. As he cried out to God, he became angry and killed him, saying, “A fellow participant

in Alexander’s impending death you shall be, and end your life confessing your faith in martyrdom.” He also ordered the brave Alexander to be hung up and scraped. While he was being scraped, he cried out, saying, “I am a Christian.” He ordered them to tear him still more. While he was being scraped, he formed the sign of the cross in his mind. Raising his eyes to heaven, he said, “Blessed are you, Lord God of our fathers, who, through the most valiant struggles, have made your servant Alexander steadfast in knowing you. See how you have brought the torture inflicted by the vile Antoninus to shame.” Hearing this, the governor ordered them to tear him again and pour vinegar mixed with salt over him, and to rub his wounds with cloth, to see whether he could force him by these tortures to offer sacrifice. But he again said in a loud voice, “Are you not ashamed, O torturer, of the evils you have committed and of pleasing demons? For if there were no human craftsmanship, you would have no god. But you, lacking understanding and bearing their likeness, are blind; you cling to the blind and have blind hopes. For what you saw a short time ago being forged with hammers and shaped with an axe, you have now set

up and call it a god. Therefore I will not obey you, nor will your terrors or your tortures frighten me. For I have God, the King of all ages, protecting me.” As he was saying this, the wounds from his flaying ran together, so that all his flesh was laid bare. All those standing there were astonished and said, “How does this man endure it?” When holy Alexander would not heed the governor’s persuasion, nor his coercion, nor his blows, nor his anger, the governor, the princeps, said, “Alexander, abandon your folly, obey, and sacrifice to the gods, and you will be the emperor’s friend.” He answered him, for his heart was turned toward God. The sound of a voice was heard [?] on the right and on the left, saying: “Take courage and be strong, Alexander, for my name’s sake. For I will deliver you from every torture and from the governor’s hands.” When the voice was heard, everyone was astonished and said, “Where does this voice come from?” Dalmatius the princeps became frightened and prodded Alexander, saying, “What is this voice that has come to you?” Then Alexander again made the sign of the cross by the grace of God. Beginning at his forehead, he made the sign of the cross over his whole body, saying, “Lord,

Almighty, blessed are you, and may your name be glorified, you who this present day, for your servant’s everlasting joy, have bestowed as a gift. And fill your servant’s soul with your goodness, and show the lawless and godless Antoninus and Dalmatius that you are the God of the Christians and that you reward those who put their trust in you.” Then Antoninus said again, “Alexander, sacrifice to the gods.” Alexander said, “I told you that I will not sacrifice to your gods, which are worthless, deaf, and blind.” Antoninus said, “How long will you blaspheme and refuse to do the emperor’s will? Keep yourself safe and sound from every wound. You are of noble birth; do not bring yourself low.” Alexander said, “I marvel at how foolishly you behave in calling them gods. How can these be gods, when they neither see nor feel nor smell? Yet you cling to them, having abandoned the living and true God and his only-begotten Son, Jesus Christ, who exists and existed before the ages, and you put your trust in pagan temples and unclean demons. So do whatever you wish, for I have told you that I am a Christian,

and your tortures do not touch me.” Antoninus said to his servants, “Light a fire, take him down from the wooden frame, and throw him into the fire, so that the fire may destroy him.” When the fire had been lit, Alexander was led forward, guided by two angels, who went into the fire with him and scattered the flames. Standing in the middle of the furnace, Alexander said, “Holy are you, O God, who in your divinity have sent down to poor Alexander help from heaven, to show that all things are subject to you. Even the blazing tongues of flame, which could not withstand the entrance of your warriors or your fearful and awe-inspiring command, have died down around me, but they scorch the mind of the lawless and impious man.” The governor became enraged and ordered him to be brought out. He said to him, “Sacrifice to the gods, so that I may spare you and send you to the emperor with great honor.” Alexander said, “You command me to sacrifice and abandon the truth, so that I may become the friend of a man subject to the same weaknesses as I am.” and I shall become an enemy of God who made me, and instead of incorruptible things, corruption

I shall gain. But rather let me disregard a man subject to the same passions as I am, who is alive today and dies tomorrow, and fear him who exists forever and existed before all things, who has prepared for the faithful things that no eye has seen and no ears have heard. Antoninus said, “Well! You have not only scorned the gods, but have also reviled the emperors. Therefore I shall have the beasts tear out your lungs while you are still alive.” Alexander said, “Once, twice, and many times I have told you that for Christ’s sake I do not fear your tortures. For they do not touch me. For if I had not known what is said: ‘You shall not put the Lord your God to the test.’ Having pledged myself to God, how can I return to the foolish and useless faith of demons, when the Lord has said that those who believe in them shall be like them, deaf and motionless? But I tell you again: devise, O tormentor, the greatest tortures you have, so that at least in this way you may learn that they are powerless, not only against me alone, but against all who endure hardship for his name’s sake.” Antoninus said, “Now I know that you sustain yourself by sorcery and much demonic possession. Those words expose you:

you are not suffering for the sake of Christ, of whom you speak, but you practice sorcery and deceive everyone.” Alexander said, “May it be your lot, you defiler, filled with such deeds, to rule with your father the devil. For to me, to live is Christ, and to die is gain.” Antoninus said, “Let him be taken to the arena, to the beasts.” And as soon as he entered, with the governor seated, he made the sign of the cross, raised his eyes to heaven, and said in a loud voice, “Quickly carry out, you ungodly man, you most impious of all, Antoninus the tormentor, the will of your father Satan. For I am ready, protected by the sign of Christ, to scorn your short-lived tortures.” When he had said this, they opened the beasts’ enclosure, and a lion came out roaring. And just as a loving father welcomes his child, so the lion ran up and leaped upon the righteous man, placed its paws beneath his arms, licked the righteous man’s sweat, and gazed at him, asking for God’s direction, so that the people might perhaps understand. As the lion groaned in this way, the keeper of the beasts opened the enclosure again, and another lion came out and fell at the saint’s feet, gazing into his face. And there came out
